speakeroldname: Mr. W. B. Nesbitt (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subtopic: IRAN-ANNOUNCEMENT OF GRANT TO ASSIST EARTHQUAKE VICTIMS
speechtext:
Following the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on April 26 concerning the recent earthquake in Iran, hon. members will wish to know that on the recommendation of the Canadian Red Cross Society a grant of $10,000 has been made from the international relief fund to assist the unfortunate victims of the disaster. These funds are being sent by the Canadian Red Cross Society to the league of Red Cross Societies in Geneva for the purchase of urgently required medicines and emergency supplies.
We are keeping in close touch with the situation in Iran through the Canadian representative in Tehran and with the Canadian Red Cross Society in case further assistance of this kind may prove appropriate.

speechtext:
On Tuesday the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) directed two questions with regard to Canada's bid for the world's fair in 1967 to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who said the questions could more properly be answered by myself.
The first question asked if the house could be informed whether the mayor of Montreal had been invited as an official representative to the conference. In reply I may say that the federal government is anxious for the inclusion in its delegation to the bureau of international exhibitions meeting on May 5 of representatives from both the province of Quebec and the city of Montreal, and we have so indicated through appropriate channels. However, up to the present we are not aware who will represent the city of Montreal.
Inquiries of the Ministry
In the second part of the hon. member's question he asked why the Postmaster General had announced in Montreal that Canada has a slim chance of having the fair. I draw his attention immediately to the fact that the use of the word "slim" was by the newspaper headline writer, and was not my own word at all. I did say that the sudden entry into the bureau of seven countries which have consistently supported the U.S.S.R. in its international relations has made the position of Canada and Austria, which are the only other two countries seeking the fair, more difficult. I think this is obvious, since the choice between the U.S.S.R., Austria and Canada will be made by the bureau based on the votes of its member states, and the hon. member is quite conversant with the voting practices.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps it will not surprise you when I assure you that I have none of the fear of repetition that seems to be in the mind of the Minister of Public Works. Not only have I no fear of repetition, but in view of the scant impression which seems to have been made on the mind of the minister by the debate which took place at the resolution stage it seems to me that a certain amount of repetition is called for, and urgently called for.
At the time the resolution preceding this bill was before the committee, namely on March 29, my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition set out, as recorded on page 2562 of Hansard, the position of the Liberal opposition on this bill. I want to repeat, not in the same words precisely but in substance, what was said by the Leader of the Opposition at that time. I do this because we on this side of the house are constantly being taunted by the government with the statement that we have no alternatives to suggest to the policies which are put forward by the government.
I want to make it abundantly clear that in this matter we have an alternative. We have an alternative which has been put clearly before the house and the country, an alternative which goes some part of the way, but not the whole distance, that hon. gentlemen who now occupy the treasury benches, notably the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), suggested it should go when the previous government were in office.

Trans-Canada Highway Act
Put very briefly, the position of the Liberal party of Canada in this matter is that owing to the disability under which they suffer with respect to transportation, the government of Canada should pay in the Atlantic provinces, and in the Atlantic provinces only, 90 per cent of the cost of building this national undertaking.
The first statement on behalf of the Leader of the Opposition was made before March 31, 1958, in these words. This was a statement issued from the office of the Leader of the Opposition:
In reply to a request about the scale of assistance contemplated in the Liberal program to provide special assistance for the building of trunk highways in the Atlantic provinces, Mr. Pearson stated that what he had in mind was the assumption by the federal government of 90 per cent of the cost of completing the trans-Canada highway in the four Atlantic provinces and the earliest possible discussion with the governments of those provinces about the routes of other key trunk highways which would be eligible for federal assistance.
As the Leader of the Opposition stated when he spoke here on March 29, that continues to be the policy of the Liberal opposition. Moreover, when he spoke on that occasion, the Leader of the Opposition quoted a statement by the present Minister of Justice when he was sitting on this side of the house on April 16, 1956. He said, as reported on page 2942 of Hansard of that date:
I said a few words prior to the adjournment on that day in which I had just got to the point where I was seeking to demonstrate that the proposal now before the house-
That is the proposal which is now before the house, I would remind the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Public Works, because there has been no change whatever by the present government from the scheme put forward at that time.
-is neither adequate to ensure the completion of the trans-Canada highway by the date mentioned in the resolution, namely, December 31, 1960, nor is it fair-
I hope the Minister of Public Works will mark these words.
-as between provinces which are participating members under the trans-Canada highway agreement.
So here we have the Minister of Justice when he was sitting on this side of the house saying that this legislation was not "fair as between provinces". Those are his words; yet he is now participating in a government which brings forward an extension of precisely the same legislation without changing anything in it except the date of completion of the road.
What accounts for this extraordinary change in view? I could go on and quote the Minister of Transport who, speaking with that moderation with which he always spoke when

he sat on this side of the house, carefully weighing every word, so characteristic of that hon. gentleman in those days, had this to say as reported on page 2955 of Hansard for April 16, 1956:
I think that we in this parliament, particularly the government, must face up to the hard, cold fact that if this highway is to be built within the foreseeable future, the federal government must assume the financial responsibility for its construction and stop playing around with makeshift methods of trying to get it built.
I repeat; "must stop playing around with makeshift methods", said the present Minister of Transport in 1956. I assume there is still a little collective responsibility left in the government in 1960, although after the display of the day before yesterday one sometimes doubts it. If there is any collective responsibility the Minister of Transport is equally responsible with the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Justice for the legislation now before the house. What did the Minister of Transport call it when he sat on this side? It was a "makeshift method". This Liberal makeshift method is the Tory policy to build the trans-Canada highway.
That is the situation, sir. I have no doubt that the Minister of Public Works, who is like a Bourbon who learns nothing

I do not know about the forgetting part, but he is half a Bourbon-will get up after I am finished speaking, and I am sure he will say, "Well, you didn't do it. Why didn't you do it?"
Well, sir, why did not we do it? We started this trans-Canada highway in 1949 on a 50-50 basis, and this was quite a departure from the previous policy in this connection. It was a pioneering venture undertaken as the result of a decision made at the national Liberal convention of 1948 and implemented by the government of Mr. St. Laurent after the election of 1949. It was a very progressive step, but it was only a step; and when in 1956 the government found that this great project was not being completed at anything like the rate we felt it should be, we made an improvement in the formula, an improvement which provided that 90 per cent of the cost should be paid for 10 per cent of the highway.
I was a member of the government when that decision was made and was of course bound by that decision, and I defended it. However, I do not mind admitting that even at that time I would have liked to go a bit further, and we found even after that change that the progress was not as rapid as it should have been. We also found that the rate of progress was very different in different provinces. In the prairie provinces, where

the problems of building were not nearly so great and where the road was in fact the main road across the province anyway, they were getting ahead very rapidly. But in other parts of Canada, for one reason or another into which I will not bother entering here, the progress was very slow, notably in the province of Ontario, and for that it is hard to find any excuse whatsoever.
At any rate, Mr. Winters came in here and proposed, and parliament agreed, to pay 90 per cent of the cost of 10 per cent of the highway. Of course the provinces had the chance to choose the most difficult 10 per cent, and I would guess most of them did so.
In order to speed things up, we in the Liberal party came to the conclusion by 1958, when we held our national convention, that even this would not get the road in the Atlantic provinces completed within a reasonable time. Why? It was because those provinces could not afford, out of their annual revenues, to devote enough money to this particular project. In fact in Nova Scotia they had barely started. The view taken by the government of Nova Scotia through the early years after 1949 was that this road, because it was not the main highway in the province and because there were other roads in the province serving the same areas, did not have the same priority from the provincial point of view as other roads did. In fact an agreement was not entered into for several years.
The plain fact is that while from a national standpoint this road is, in my opinion, very important, in some of the provinces-Ontario, for example-it does not assume the same importance. I know about this, in the case of Nova Scotia, because I was in the gallery of the Nova Scotia legislature myself a couple of years ago and heard the minister of highways say that they did not feel they could give a high priority to the trans-Canada highway over other roads for which they also had to pay.
It is not for me to say why this situation should exist, but it certainly does, as experience has shown. Even, as in the case of the province of Newfoundland, where the highway is the main road in the province, there is still not enough in the provincial budget that can be devoted to the completion of this project after all the other essential expenditures have been made. That is why we took the view at the national Liberal convention of 1958 that additional help should be given to the provinces with respect to the construction of roads in the light of the fact that considerable provision had been made elsewhere to assist railway construction. In the Atlantic provinces, except 79951-0-212J
Trans-Canada Highway Act for one small line in New Brunswick, railways were no longer the answer to transportation problems, and roads obviously were. However, railways were still being built-very long railways in the province of Quebec, and considerable branch lines in Ontario, in addition to railways in all the prairie provinces and in British Columbia- for virtually all of which very substantial assistance was provided by parliament.

There was nothing exceptional about that; it is the general practice in all the provinces.
However, we took the view that since roads were the real need, roads rather than railways, which were helped elsewhere, had become a matter of national importance, because we in the Liberal party were of the opinion that it is a national responsibility to try to maintain conditions across Canada as nearly equal as it is possible to maintain them. The Minister of Justice said this legislation which he is now helping to sponsor was unfair. It is unfair; there is no question about that. It is very unfair, and that is one of the reasons why we adopted this proposal which was put forward in 1958.
My hon. friend from Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) in a speech he made on March 31, I think it was, made a masterly analysis of the situation which gave one a real insight into the per capita costs and the difficulties encountered by the various provinces. It was a masterly speech which it would be wrong of me to repeat to the house at any length but in my opinion the most striking of all the many remarkable statistics my hon. friend put on the record was the comparison between British Columbia and Newfoundland.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) can relax, because I am going to admit

Trans-Canada Highway Act the point he wants made. We all recognize that the difficulties of building roads in British Columbia are great, that they are probably greater in some areas of that province than they are in any other province. But they are not very much greater than they are in the province of Newfoundland, and there is this additional difficulty with which I shall deal. The figures show that 13 per cent of the total length of this trans-Canada highway is in British Columbia and 13 per cent is in Newfoundland. In other words there is about the same length in each of the two provinces. However, the cost of the provincial share has to be spread among less than half a million people in Newfoundland as compared with about two million people in British Columbia.

speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for his diversion. It is almost worthy of the Prime Minister.
The point from which I refuse to be diverted, because it is an extreme example, is this. Here we have a road which we are building as a national undertaking right across Canada. Thirteen per cent of it is in the most westerly province and 13 per cent in the most easterly province, but there are at least four times as many people in the westernmost province to pay their share. Then, to compare incomes, the westernmost province enjoys the highest average income in the whole country, while unhappily-I am sorry to have to say it, but it is true-the easternmost province has the lowest. No wonder the Minister of Justice when he sat on this side of the house and was free to express his opinion said this situation was unfair. It is unfair, and that is why we changed our policy -and we are not ashamed of the fact that we learn things.

speechtext: Why did you change it in 1958, after you were defeated?

speechtext:
Because we did' not change it before. That seems to me to be a good reason, and I am not ashamed to admit that I have changed my mind about a good many things. Why did we change the 50-50 formula to the 90-10 formula? It was because we had

learned something. The Minister of Transport, when he sat over here, said the whole road should be paid for by the treasury of Canada. What has happened to him since he went to sit over there?

speechtext: He has learned something and changed his mind, too.

speechtext:
He has learned that he is not the boss. He has learned that the Minister of Finance would just say no. He was not the only one to offer hopes. I have here the text of a very interesting television performance put on by the Minister of Public Works in the city of St. John's on October 19, 1959. That was the same day the minister had the satisfaction of presiding over the opening of a public building in the city of St. John's which was at that time, I think, the largest building in that city, and which was built by a Liberal government. On that day the minister made a very favourable impression in St. John's, I might say. I happened to be there, and I had the pleasure of seeing him on television. I thought he put on a very good performance. However, I thought I should like to have the text of his performance, because I anticipated that the day might come when it ought to be recorded in a less perishable form than on television. There are bits of it I should like the house to read, and I am sure the minister would be delighted to hear them. Mr. Jamieson, the interlocutor, had asked the minister some questions about term 29. I am not going to repeat those questions, because I realize they would not be relevant to this debate, though perhaps I could make them relevant if I were challenged. Mr. Jamieson said this:
In other words, I gather that this is another way of saying what was emphasized earlier-
That was in the minister's previous answer.
-that in so far as the federal government is concerned, it is not a matter of wiping out Newfoundland's special needs, but that there is still recognition of the fact that we do have special needs in this province.
This is the minister's reply:
Very, very much so, and there's no one, I think, who appreciates the needs of Newfoundland more than the dominion government at Ottawa.
There might be two views about that matter, but this is what the minister said. Then a little later on-there are several other questions which are not relevant to the trans-Canada highway-I come to this question:
Well, sir, something else that came up at the press conference this morning was the question of the over-all attitude of the federal government here with regard to the trans-Canada highway. Again, this is of great concern to us in Newfoundland, and I think you had some comments that the paving, in the park at any rate, would be done next year.

This was in 1959. Here is the minister's reply:
Yes, the part that we are 100 per cent responsible for is your wonderful park-
I am extremely pleased that the minister recognized that the park the Liberal government established in the year 1957 is the wonderful park that we know it is. He said:
Yes, the part that we are 100 per cent responsible for is your wonderful park, and that 26 miles will be completed early in 1960.
I can tell the minister that was very good news. I have since learned that tenders have been called, and I hope he will not be too long in deciding to let the contracts. Some of us expect to ride over that road this summer, early in 1960, if we can get away from here. Then he went on to give some figures of the cost, and went on to explain the cost-sharing formula which is well known to the house and which it would be an imposition to repeat. Then Mr. Jamieson said this:
Sir, I am aware of the fact, of course, that you can't discuss matters of government policy.
I do not know why. When I was a minister I did not hesitate to discuss matters of government policy, but perhaps the minister is more discreet in this matter. I continue with the quotation:
There has been a suggestion, in other parts of Canada as well, that perhaps the whole basis for the construction of the trans-Canada highway might have to be changed. Is there any likelihood, or is there any suggestion that the whole policy might be reviewed?
The minister's reply was as follows:
Oh, well, I think the policy ought to be reviewed.
I emphasize that statement. He said:
Oh, well, I think the policy ought to be reviewed ... At the end of 1960, the trans-Canada act runs out and certainly we can't see the provinces left in the lurch, and this is a tremendous project, particularly in Newfoundland where you really want to have a trans-Canada highway go from sea to sea, and we're anxious to co-operate and I am sure that some form of extension will be arranged and I trust it will be satisfactory to your provincial government.
I am not seeking to suggest for one minute that the minister in any of those words went one iota beyond the bill that is now before us, because that would be unfair. But I suggest that the average Newfoundlander listening to those words would get the impression that when the new legislation came along we were going to get a better deal than we had before.
The minister did not say so. I am not saying that he said so. However, I am saying that even I, with all my experience and with all my suspicion of the minister, thought there might be some faint chance that these words were meant to be more than just a hope.
Trans-Canada Highway Act Then the best this government could do was to go on precisely along the lines of the previous government which they are so fond of condemning so much of the time and which they promised, of course, not merely to replace on the treasury benches but to change all those things that were being done so inadequately.
One would have thought that one of the things that would most assuredly have been changed would be something which the Minister of Justice, of all men, said was not fair, and particularly when so influential a member of the government as the Minister of Transport said the whole thing should be paid for out of the federal treasury.

In this particular instance that is the thing they are doing. I was greatly disappointed by the speech that was made in this debate by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Mc-Cleave); I do not know whether I should call him the taller or the junior member for Halifax. I refer to the hon. member for Halifax who sits on this side of the house. The hon. member for Halifax said in effect [DOT]-and if he thinks I am being unfair to him I am quite willing to read the extracts from Hansard-that because the Atlantic provinces grant, for which all of us in the Atlantic provinces who have any sense are very grateful; it is the only thing we have to be grateful to this government for-the federal government had no other obligations in the highway field to the provinces, although the hon. member expressed the hope that some time or other they would build a road into Halifax. I might say that if he and enough people like him had supported us that road would have been started by now, because that is one of the trunk roads that it would be part of Liberal policy to build and one of the most important of them, quite obviously.
But I would remind the hon. member for Halifax that a much different attitude was taken by the Conservative party in 1957, at

Trans-Canada Highway Act the time that hon. gentleman was elected to this house. At that time, although I have not seen the list of names, I imagine the hon. member for Halifax was present at the historic meeting in Moncton when the great charter of the Tory party for the Atlantic provinces was drawn up. At that time the Atlantic provinces were promised Atlantic provinces grants or something equivalent to them. Special adjustment grants they were called in this document, and I take it that is the same thing.
But they were also promised-and it is No. 4 of the Atlantic resolutions-the "adjustment of freight rates and provision of transportation facilities to allow our producers reasonable access to the markets of Canada". The only adjustment in freight rates has been an adjustment upward of 17 per cent, and then 10 per cent was taken off afterwards. So that the only adjustment we have had so far is 7 per cent up, nothing down. It just says "adjustment" here in the Atlantic resolutions. People were intended to believe that it would be an adjustment down, not up, but that is what we have. As for the provision of other transportation facilities, we have had nothing whatever.
That is the whole point. It does not seem to me that any Tory member of this house who subscribes to this Atlantic resolution should be satisfied to support and vote for this bill in its present form, because certainly people in the Atlantic provinces were led to believe by everything that was said before hon. gentlemen opposite attained office that the situation would be different.
There is just one other thing I wish to say about this matter. I regret, and I think every Canadian who really believes that this is a great national project in which all parts of the country should participate regrets very much, that the government of the province of Quebec up to now has not seen fit to participate. I hope, if certain events that many of us look for should come about, that the situation will be changed before too long. This is one reason I am glad that at any rate, if no other change is made in this bill, the time is being extended so that our fellow citizens in Quebec who pay their share in taxes for this road, will get their share of the benefits to which they are entitled and which it is no fault of this parliament, and particularly of this party, that they have not had long ago.
But I do say this, sir. I am rather astonished after the constitutional expose made to this house by the Solicitor General the day before yesterday in which he told us with respect


to another piece of legislation, and perhaps I should quote his exact words from page 3288 of Hansard:
The Liberal legislation was made applicable only to nine provinces out of ten.

The Solicitor General is a member of the government. He shared the responsibility with the Minister of Justice who said this bill was unfair, and with the Minister of Transport who said it should be on an entirely different basis, and with the Secretary of State for External Affairs who, when he was over here, said the country could afford to spend far more on this road.
That is their record. They all come in here together and jointly recommend the renewal of this Liberal legislation unchanged except for the dates. That is what they are doing, these gentlemen on the treasury benches. Well, of course, you know-

I want to say one more thing about this matter, and it is pretty fundamental. I do think, sir, that experience with the trans-Canada highway and with some of those other 50-50 sharing arrangements-I said this the last time this bill was before the house and wish to say it again- has shown, as the Minister of Justice said when he was over here, this is a very unfair way to have federal financial participation. It creates a great incentive for provinces that are wealthy or provinces that are favourably situated to accept those proposals and get money out of the taxpayers generally, and it often imposes programs upon other provinces, because of the incentive of some federal money, that perhaps they would not give the first priority to if they were managing their own affairs themselves.
I do think that normally-I say "normally" -the federal government should not make conditional payments to provinces to further provincial objects. I believe it is far better to increase the amount that is paid under equalization payments and leave the provinces generally free and autonomous to carry out their functions as they and their electors see fit.
I was fully in agreement with the Minister of Public Works when he suggested that we should go slow on a second trans-Canada highway and on some of those other projects, not because I object in principle to a second trans-Canada highway, but because I think the whole financial basis of the project should be looked at from two aspects, the financial and also the constitutional basis. I do not mean the phony constitutional basis of the Solicitor General; I mean the genuine constitutional basis, that is to say whether it is really desirable for the federal treasury to be paying half the cost of provincial services when they are really just provincial services,
Trans-Canada Highway Act instead of leaving the responsibility to the provincial electors, the provincial legislators and the provincial governments, and putting them, through equalization payments that have no strings attached, in a position to do it themselves.
I think this is doubly important, sir, so long as we are going to have the situation that has now existed for 10 years in the case of the trans-Canada highway, where one province with almost one third of the population is having to bear a share of the cost of this project while getting no benefit from it. I say again, it is no fault of ours, it is no fault of this parliament, but it is a fact. It is a fact that we cannot escape, and I think we should be more careful about the proliferation of schemes of this sort unless we are really sure there will be universal participation right across the country, and unless we are convinced that the division of cost is really equitable, as it certainly is not in this case.
There is no doubt that the greatest beneficiary by far of this trans-Canada highway legislation is the province of Ontario. The province of Ontario has by far the longest stretch of the road, and what we are doing is taxing all the people of Canada to pay out of the federal treasury half plus 90 per cent of the cost of 10 per cent of that road in the province of Ontario. I think it was a good thing to do, because we need a trans-Canada highway. I do not question that we need it very badly, but it should be right across Canada and not part way across. I say that the proposal to extend this kind of sharing into normal provincial services is very dangerous and, as the Minister of Justice has said, it is a very unfair way to do it. I think we should look at it with the greatest possible care.
I would hope that at the federal-provincial conference which is to take place in July this whole question will be considered in relation to the question of equalization. I cannot help but feel that if we could increase the equalization grants, which is fairer because it puts the poorer provinces on a genuine level of equality with the better off ones, and then leave the provinces to do their own job in their own way, we would be acting more in the genuine spirit of confederation and would be distributing the money more fairly. If there are to be more projects of this kind I hope the division of financial cost will be more along the lines of the hospital insurance plan, where there was not only a 50-50 division but some account was also taken of the burden upon the province and its capacity to pay.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I must express our disappointment with regard to the limited amendments contained in the bill now before us. After the lengthy debate at the resolution stage we had expected that the government would agree to accept a number of amendments that were offered by the opposition. However, we have to deal with the amendments as contained in the bill now before us.
I regret very much that the minister of highways of the province of British Columbia did not assist us at the resolution stage or even before the resolution stage. Unfortunately he came to Ottawa after the resolution stage had already passed, and he then attempted to persuade the government as to what kind of amendments it should make to the Trans-Canada Highway Act. I believe that as a legislator and cabinet minister he should have known a little better, and should have realized that if he wanted to have any major influence on the policy decisions of the government the time to approach the government was at least not later than the end of the debate at the resolution stage, so the government might have taken cognizance of whatever representation he wished to make before the debate on second reading began.
I regret that the legislation before us will permit the richest provinces of Canada to continue to procrastinate with regard to making their contribution to the completion of what will be our first trans-Canada highway. I should have liked to see in the bill some kind of penalty by way of reduced percentages payable by the federal government to those wealthy areas of Canada that have been standing idly by. I have special reference here to my own province of British Columbia and even more particularly to the province of Ontario. I do not think the House of Commons can continue to encourage indefinitely procrastination on the part of these two richest areas of Canada by continuous postponement of the termination date beyond which the federal contribution will no longer be payable.
We do not intend to oppose the further postponement of that date by three years


now being sought by the government. However, we feel that if British Columbia and Ontario do not begin at a very early date to show evidence of more honest intentions to complete their portions of the trans-Canada highway, then the whole basis of federal sharing should be given a very serious review so that an incentive for early completion on the part of the wealthier areas of Canada may be contained in the legislation.
I note that the permissible amount of government expenditure is to be raised from $350 million to $400 million, and I regret very much that at least a portion of the additional $50 million will have to be spent for the completion of the federal government's share of the trans-Canada highway, namely that portion running through our national parks. Much as we regret that some provinces are being very slow in completing their share of the work, we regret even more having to make the observation that the federal government has also been unduly slow. It should have completed its share of the highway, the mileage through the national parks, long before any of the provinces should have been expected to complete their share of the work.
I also regret that in the bill before us there is no amendment to enable the government to undertake the building of an alternative western route as a second trans-Canada highway. It is obvious that the decision of the government is rather confirmed by now, and that the building of an additional national highway will have to wait until the slowest of the provinces has completed its portion of the first trans-Canada highway. In my opinion the lack of any such authority in the bill now before us constitutes discrimination against the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta which, if they have not already done so, have about completed their share of the first highway. The lack of a suitable amendment in the bill indicates that they will have to continue to wait indefinitely before they can proceed with other major highway building unless, of course, they are willing to pay the whole cost themselves.
The official spokeman for the Liberal party introduced a rather novel idea as to how the poorer provinces of Canada might be aided and encouraged in building their portions of the trans-Canada highway a little more rapidly. I have great reservations as to the remedy he proposed. He referred to my attitude with regard to the national hospital insurance plan, and attempted to compare the arrangements arrived at in that regard with the arrangements that exist under the Trans-Canada Highway Act.

I believe there are reasons that obtain in the hospital insurance field for the formula that was adopted there that do not apply in this particular case. I am very concerned about the remedy that was offered, because I am not too sure that this is the way in which the Atlantic provinces can be helped to meet their responsibilities. Is the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate advocating that this policy which he suggested might be made applicable in many fields of federal legislation? If so, perhaps he would be quite happy to see varying rates of old age pensions being paid in different parts of Canada.
I believe that when this parliament legislates it must legislate under rules and conditions that are applicable to all parts of Canada without discrimination. I am not saying that cognizance should not be taken of the ability of the provinces to meet their responsibilities, but I feel that the federal government should see it is not in the form of discriminatory legislation. This situation should be met by changes in the financial arrangements between the two levels of government. If aid is needed in this field by these eastern governments, that is the time and place where financial resources must be made available to these governments in such a way that they can take their proper place and receive the benefits of specific legislation offered by the parliament of Canada.
I am saying this, Mr. Speaker, with a particular complaint in mind. I regret that in the amendment now before us the government has not seen fit to enact into law a policy decision that was announced in this house by the previous Liberal government. This policy was that if federal money were being used in the building of any portion of the trans-Canada highway, tolls could not be imposed. We in B.C. had serious complaints and differences of opinion in years gone by, I will admit, with the government that is no longer in office. We wanted a federal contribution, for instance, toward the construction of the Oak street bridge, and we wanted to recover part of our contribution by the imposition of tolls. The former minister of public works, Hon. Robert Winters, made it very clear in this house that the government was not prepared to make a contribution to the building of a bridge within a province, or any part of the trans-Canada highway, if tolls were to be imposed and the provincial government enabled to recover its share of the cost thereby.
We heard the same argument again at the time of the building of the new Port Mann bridge. The policy of the federal government was reiterated, and we had to abide by the decision of the federal government in this
Trans-Canada Highway Act regard. The reason I would have loved to have that policy announcement included in the amendment now before us is that I notice this policy is not being followed in the province of Nova Scotia. I have received this information since the resolution stage. In a return tabled on April 4 last the Minister of Transport admitted that up to March 1, 1960 the federal government had expended $20,157,201 on the building of the Canso causeway, but the Nova Scotia government is not committed, under any conditions, to the spending of more than $5.5 million. However, the Nova Scotia government are allowed to recover whatever expenditures they may have made by imposing a toll of 75 cents- and that is a high toll-on people using the Canso causeway.
I believe the federal government owes a responsibility to the other areas of Canada that have not been granted this right. It is right to insist that whatever agreement may have been made with the government of Nova Scotia, that agreement be so amended that it forbids Nova Scotia to do this, or that there be written into the legislation a clause whereby any provincial government shall have the right to recover any of its contribution by the collection of tolls on any public undertaking to which the federal government has made a contribution.
I believe that if the people of British Columbia are going to be denied the right to collect tolls, and I agree they ought to be denied that right, we should ask that the same rule of law be made applicable to the people of Nova Scotia using the Canso causeway, which is part of the trans-Canada highway. At one time the Pattullo bridge was not part of the trans-Canada highway, but immediately upon it being made a part of the highway we had to desist from the collection of tolls. We did so, and the bridge has been toll-free ever since. The Port Mann bridge, similarly, should be a toll-free bridge.
Let me say again that I am sure we are aware of the fact that the government of Nova Scotia may need these revenues. They may need them in the worst possible way, just as the hon. member was able to outline the needs of the government of Newfoundland for vast sums of additional revenue if it is going to be able to play its proper role in the development of its economy. However, we feel that the proper method of helping these Atlantic provinces is by substantial increases in their revenues at a time when the federal tax-sharing agreements are up for revision.
We regret that the amendment before us, in the light of the need for national development, in the light of the need for national

Trans-Canada Highway Act unity and the part that highways have played in that regard, in the light ot supplying employment and reducing unemployment in Canada, has not made more allowance for the development of the Canadian economy.

speechtext: I have great pleasure in rising to speak on the amendment which is before the house. Before doing so I should like to make one comment. I take a vastly different position from that of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. In my opinion if this country is to be developed, and particularly west of the great lakes, we must have highways. We cannot wait forever to have these highways. Therefore, instead of adopting the thought emanating from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate this afternoon, I think we must have a policy which will provide federal assistance for the building of additional trans-Canada highways.

Does the hon. gentleman think that we east of the great lakes and east of the St. Lawrence do have to wait forever? That is what I was complaining about.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I did not say that.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
But you inferred it.
Mr. Speaker, turning now to the question of trans-Canada highways, I live in that part of western Canada known as southwestern Alberta, about which I wish to speak briefly at this time because it has a very direct bearing on the route which I believe the next trans-Canada highway should take. I refer particularly to that area in southwestern Alberta around Lethbridge, the Crowsnest

pass, Cranbrook, Nelson, Okanagan and through there-the area known as the southern route. In my remarks I shall refer to this route as the southern route.
When plans for trans-Canada highway No. 1 were being developed a decision had to be made as to whether it would go from Medicine Hat, Calgary, Banff, Lake Louise, Cranbrook and on west, or whether it would take the southern route and go through Medicine Hat, Lethbridge, Fort Macleod, Crowsnest pass, Cranbrook, Nelson and on west.
One only has to look at a map to see which is the best route and the most economical route, and which, if physical conditions and economic development were to be considered, should have been the route. But there was a lot of discussion at that time about which route it should take. Since Calgary was the largest city and Banff had the tourist attractions developing at that time, the pressure was to put it in through that way, and the southern route was left as a by-passed route.
It is about that route which I wish to speak today. I do so because the southern route is now one of the fastest developing areas in western Canada. It is the most direct route from Medicine Hat to the west coast. Not only that, but if it were developed we would have in that area tourist trade coming up from the south in greater numbers because often people on vacation have not the time to go further north. In other words, if the tourist had four or five days he could come up into Canada visit Waterton lakes, go through the Crowsnest pass and visit the scenic points in that area and we would get that tourist's dollar. At the present time we are missing that tourist's dollar.
That is only one argument in favour of having a four-lane highway through that area. However, while talking about scenery and the tourist trade I should like to emphasize one or two points. I said before that we lost out when it came to the location of highway No. 1, and we certainly should have priority for consideration of any additional trans-Canada highway to be built. Any new highway should follow the southern route through southern Alberta and the Crowsnest pass and then through sourthern British Columbia. Let me say that along that route there are such fast growing industrial cities as Lethbridge, Nelson, Cranbrook, et cetera. Then there are areas of amusement such as Waterton lakes national park, one of the finest summer and pleasure resorts not only in western Canada but, people have said, in the world. It is a place where the tourist can go and rest and be quiet, and that is of course often the feature the tourist puts first.

Then there is the Frank slide at the eastern end, of the Crowsnest pass which is one of the most scenic spots existing in western Canada. It is the place where a mountain fell across the valley covering the town of Frank and the railroad and the highway, and it is a scenic spot which I am sure any tourist once having seen it will never forget. The tourist could go on through the Crowsnest pass, Fernie, the beautiful Okanagan lakes, and so on. I need not recite to this house why the southern route should not be chosen from the point of scenery.
Let me now turn to the industrial side. At the British-American plant at Pincher Creek a large proportion, I should say, of the natural gas coming into Ontario originates in that field. Then there are the scrubbing plants, industrial development, and more industrial development is in the making. Then going through the Crowsnest pass will be the 36-inch pipe line exporting gas to the United States. There are other lines criss-crossing to join up with the trans-Canada pipe line. In other words, we have in that area an industry now in existence and a great deal more development in the offing. Step across the line from Alberta into British Columbia and you have there the development of the Columbia basin. What need is there for me to give any more reasons for asking and pressing for first consideration of this southern route, the shortest route, as the next trans-Canada highway?
Before leaving the question of the tourist trade, I might say that there has recently been set up the Crowsnest pass historic sites and development board. That board, or it may be called a society, is doing everything possible to develop the beauties of the Crowsnest pass area and when it is fully developed it will be a tourist's paradise. With regard to accommodation we have plenty of excellent accommodation and more will be built as time goes on. Therefore as the route where a second trans-Canada highway should be put to accommodate the tourist traffic and industry, the southern route has everything in its favour and the area is losing millions of dollars waiting for this development.
Let me say in conclusion that we have been by-passed by those who planned the No. 1 highway 15 or 20 years ago. I do not think the Minister of Public Works or the government should be left to find this out for themselves. I feel it is my duty, since I represent the Fort Macleod, and Crowsnest pass areas to bring this to the attention of the government. It is a matter which would be given serious and first consideration, and I urge the government when it is studying the construction of a future trans-Canada
Trans-Canada Highway Act highway to give full weight to representations in favour of developing this southern route. I go one step further and suggest that in view of the fact that this route was by-passed in the planning stage of the present No. 1 highway it is appropriate that we on the southern route should press for construction of this route first and foremost, and the people of southern Alberta will look with disfavour on any other choice, unless the southern route is developed either first or simultaneously.

The very reason I rose before you did, Your Honour, was to raise this matter. Until you yourself spoke, no one had raised any question about the relevancy of what was being said. Trans-Canada Highway Act have been perfectly in order on the resolution stage when we are discussing whether or not there should be such a bill as is proposed. maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: May I, then, just add this? I cannot understand why neither Your Honour nor anyone else raised any objection to what was said by the previous speaker. If it cannot, then I want the same privilege as was accorded to the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. speechtext:
Having listened to the remarks about what is, and what is not in order during discussion of this bill on second reading, may I say that I did not have the opportunity to speak during the resolution stage.
I had intended, today, to make some comments with regard to a second trans-Canada highway but since you have ruled, sir, that that would be out of order, I shall have to refrain from doing so and try to keep within your direction. However, what I wished most particularly to say on behalf of the part of New Brunswick that I represent would deal, more or less, with a subject which would probably be not strictly in order on second reading. It has been intimated that we can discuss this matter on the first item of the minister's estimates when they are before the committee.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) gave a resume of what transpired in connection with the Trans-Canada Highway Act, when he spoke on the resolution stage. He was brief at that time and he was also brief today because I think he felt that the background of the Trans-Canada Highway Act had been well covered on previous occasions. This amendment before us today is one to extend until May 31, 1964 the period during which payments may be made to the provinces and to prolong until December 31, 1963 the period in respect of which construction costs may be incurred under this act and to provide also that the aggregate of all expenditures under the act may be increased to a maximum of $400 million.
For reasons I just mentioned when I rose to speak, I shall be brief today. But at the outset I want to assure the minister of my support of this bill. I am sure that all other members of the house will also support the bill, particularly those of the Liberal party, realizing that this is Liberal legislation.
The Trans-Canada Highway Act in its present form as amended in 1956 provided that no contributions or payments were to

be made to a province after May, 1961 or in respect of any construction costs incurred after December 31, 1960. The first purpose of the bill is to extend the time limit a further period of three years. The second purpose of this bill is to increase the present limit from $350 million to $400 million. As I said, I am not going to give the background of this act which was born on December 10, 1949. From time to time it has been necessary to increase the total amount of federal contributions. Hon. members are in a general sense familiar with what has taken place since this act first came into force. The extension of the time limit to March 31, 1964 was not looked for based on the statement made by the former minister of public works when, as found in Hansard of February 24, 1959, a year ago, at page 1345, he said:
The actual problem dealt with by the legislation, amendment of which is sought, is the completion of a trans-Canada highway to join the ten provinces of this nation by a first-class road. That is our main objective. That is the objective we aim to reach by the end of 1960.
We now have an amendment seeking an extension of three years beyond 1961. It is obvious that the present Minister of Public Works did not have very much faith in his predecessor's estimates of the time of completion of the trans-Canada highway; and it is apparent that the former minister of public works was not very well advised on the progress and approximate time of completion. The present minister is planning to avoid getting into a similar situation. He is allowing himself three years for completion, perhaps on the advice of some of the provinces that money is going to be hard to find and that it will be too expensive, with the resulting slowdown of trans-Canada highway construction.
When the time limit for completion was first set out by the Liberal government, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Green), then in opposition, and who later became minister of public works in charge of the trans-Canada highway construction, said this back in the opposition days and I quote from Hansard of 1956, page 3094:
The minister-
He was referring to Hon. Mr. Winters.
-should take far more aggressive action to see that this particular gap is closed.
I think it is very difficult for us to understand why such further delay is to be granted. The gap that was referred to by the former minister of public works was a gap in the province of Ontario. The previous minister of public works questioned in 1956 the reason for the further extension. We now find the government in which he is a cabinet minister
Trans-Canada Highway Act and until recently responsible for the public works portfolio asking for a three-year term of extension to 1964.
The other change is to increase the present limit of $350 million to $400 million. Here again the previous minister of public works stated at the resolution stage of last year's amendment to this act, as found in Hansard of February 20, 1959, page 1246:
From estimates furnished by the provinces it is now considered that the total federal contributions required by the termination date of the act will be in the order of $350 million.
In fairness to the former minister and I should probably say in fairness to his staff, a more realistic figure of $371 million was tabled on the second reading of the bill. It is difficult to understand now why the public works minister of that day tabled an estimate of $371 million and on second reading of the 1959 amendment he only adds $350 million to the authority to spend.
This question also rises. Does the increase to $400 million cover expenditures in the province of Quebec up to 1964? If this province joins in the trans-Canada highway agreement I would think that this amount is not sufficient and that it would probably be necessary to seek another amendment to the act in order to cover construction of the trans-Canada highway.
It is interesting to read what the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) said as an opposition member representing the constituency of Broadview, as found at pages 2954 and 2955 of Hansard of 1956. Let me quote only part of his remarks of that day:
In short, if this highway is going to be built in the foreseeable future, the federal government must assume financial responsibility and get on with the job.
I wonder what he thinks now and I wonder what has been his thinking over the past three years as Minister of Transport, with the trans-Canada highway far from completed and the government insisting that the provinces contribute to the cost.
I recall the words of the Minister of Justice, speaking in 1956 when he was an opposition member. I was interested in his remarks because I felt they had considerable merit and offered a plan for an extended system of connecting highways. I hope you will bear with me, if I make a short quotation. I do not want to be out of order in this regard. In the 1956 debate the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) moved an amendment which reads in part as follows:
And therefore the government should take into immediate consideration with the governments of the various provinces the advisability of enlarging the scope of the existing trans-Canada highway agreements so as to develop a system of national

Trans-Canada Highway Act
highways, both east-west and north-south, financed and maintained jointly by the dominion and the provinces on an acceptable and realistic basis.
I do not want to pursue that matter having regard to the ruling just made by the Chair. However, I am looking forward to a further opportunity when the public works estimates are before this house to make certain suggestions that I feel are necessary for the economy, not only of the province of New Brunswick but of the Atlantic provinces. I have in mind something which I really think would help the economy of that area and which may have to do not only with the trans-Canada highway but also with connecting highways.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to make any extended remarks at this time on the trans-Canada highway since I expressed my opinion on this matter at the resolution stage. If I am not out of order in saying so, Mr. Speaker, I was rather interested in what was said by the hon. member who has just taken his seat and also by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Kindt). I think many of us in this house would be very happy at some time to hear expressions of what they consider should be done as far as a main network of roads across this country is concerned, rather than just one trans-Canada highway. Perhaps when the estimates of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) are before the committee it might indeed be a very good time to discuss such matters as that. I would like to have the opportunity of discussing roads in my province of Newfoundland other than the trans-Canada highway which provides the present prescribed course. But in view of the ruling that has been made, Mr. Speaker, I will try to keep to the right lane and see if I can stay in order.
First of all, I wish to say I am going to support the principle of this bill. However, I have always had the private view-I said

so when I was on the other side of the house, I say so now-and it has always been my opinion that the federal government should have built, paid for and maintained a road across this country. I had hoped that when the amendment to the Trans-Canada Highway Act was discussed in the house we might have had some change from the original act. We remember that when the act came before parliament in 1949 it was named a 50-50 deal. I have already passed my opinion on 50-50 deals and I do not propose to do so now, but it was a 50-50 deal in 1949. In 1956, when the act was first amended, there was the addition of 90 per cent of the cost of 10 per cent of the mileage. Under the new amendment, which was brought in in 1956, the federal government paid 90 per cent of 10 per cent of the total mileage, as I said. What changes could have been made? I made some suggestions in my speech at the resolution stage as to what could be done. We, too, have the suggestions contained in the platform of the Liberal party. Again I had hoped that this amendment would have contained some reference to the maintenance of this road. In some provinces I do not think we are too far from the time when the maintenance bill is going to be one that will have to be considered. I do not
Trans-Canada Highway Act know how long the pavement of the trans-Canada highway will last in all the provinces. It may be possible that in some provinces it will last for 10 years; in some other provinces it may last for 15 years and in still others it may last for 20 years. But, at any rate, the time is going to come shortly- and 20 years is not a long time in the life of a province-when a repaving job on top of annual maintenance will have to be carried out. I would hope that at some time, when this act is further amended, some consideration will be given to the maintenance of the trans-Canada highway.
I have said before that the trans-Canada highway is of particular importance to Newfoundland. For example, we have in Newfoundland a narrow gauge railway. It was a very good railway at the time it was built. During the first and second world wars it gave yeoman service to the people of Newfoundland. In the second world war particularly, when a large number of troops from the United States were stationed in the province, this railway was able to carry on very well and served the needs of that time. But I think it is apparent to most people that a narrow gauge railway is not able to provide the people of Newfoundland with the service that a wider gauge could. However, I think it is pretty evident now that we are not going to get a wide gauge railway in Newfoundland within the immediate future. When I was on the other side of the house I suggested that this railway should be widened.
If the railway is not going to be widened, then obviously there is going to be a greater burden placed on any trans-island road from Port aux Basques to St. John's. I speak of this because it gives added importance to the necessity of getting this road built and built as quickly as possible. We all know that there is going to be a federal-provincial conference in June. I hope that at that conference the trans-Canada highway will be discussed by the representatives of the federal government and of the 10 provinces. It is my hope that in that discussion of the trans-Canada highway there will be some reference to further trans-Canada highways but certainly some reference to the maintenance of the first trans-Canada highway in the years that lie immediately ahead. Otherwise the provinces are going to find themselves under the same burden in maintaining the road as they are now experiencing in building it. I have concluded the remarks I wish to make at this time, and again I say that I am going to support the principle of the bill.

Trans-Canada Highway Act ever been able to prove that this act encroached upon provincial autonomy. I also wanted to remind the house that it is urgent that the province of Quebec take advantage of it.

Trans-Canada Highway Act Second, the construction of the Metropolitan boulevard, also running from east to west in northern Montreal, is finished or nearly finished. I might perhaps let it go at that. However, having long since learned to face my responsibilities,

In joining the discussion on the subject before the house this afternoon there are a few matters I wish to bring to the attention of hon. members. In doing so I should like to extend my congratulations to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) and to his predecessor
Trans-Canada Highway Act on the fact that for the first time in all the years the trans-Canada program has been operated, it has become a truly trans-Canada highway.
Speaking earlier on this subject, hon. members of this house have stated that the trans-Canada highway ends at Vancouver. I think it is most important to point out that the trans-Canada highway has an extensive connection on Vancouver island from Victoria up to Campbell River. But even more important than the island, a link was necessary along the north shore to connect the highway to the port of Horseshoe Bay where ferries transport vehicles from the lower mainland to the highway on Vancouver island itself. This extensive gap was not recognized for many years until the present and immediately previous minister of public works determined that this section running from the Second Narrows on Burrard inlet through to Horseshoe Bay should be considered part of the trans-Canada highway.
In making these remarks I must admit it is not with any surprise that British Columbia members realize that hon. members from the rest of Canada do not recognize what the trans-Canada highway program consists of in British Columbia, for in our province we have an odd situation. Our roads, both the trans-Canada highway and the others, are not built by joint co-operation between governments; they are not even built by the province, but by a strange, garrulous and bombastic individual by the name of Gaglardi, according to his publicity. I say this to bring to the attention of the house the fact that this essential link from the Second Narrows to Horseshoe Bay is not recognized by the public as a part of the trans-Canada highway system. Again I want to pay my compliments to the minister for including this vital link in this program. I would ask again that during the meetings to take place in June with the provinces he should review the policies of co-operation with regard to the Second Narrows bridge itself, an essential link between the north shore and the south shore on Burrard inlet. I trust that in such negotiations he may be able, as I realize he would wish, to ensure that this great structure should be toll-free to the motorists and a proper part of the trans-Canada highway system.
On the subject of the trans-Canada highway routing I think it might be proper to state that while those who have not visited our beautiful west coast do not recognize it, extensive population centres exist up the

Trans-Canada Highway Act coast on the mainland, the chief community of which is the city of Powell River, home of the world's largest pulp and paper industry. Here again I would hope the minister might enter some discussion to see if it might be possible to extend the trans-Canada highway, in co-operation with the province of British Columbia, from Horseshoe Bay to Squamish, thence making the connecting link of road from Squamish to Port Mellon, thus avoiding the current necessity of a most unsatisfactory ferry service from Horseshoe Bay to Granthams Landing. Then extending the road from Port Mellon up to the Sunshine coast to join with Powell River across Jarvis inlet. I think this extension of the trans-Canada route would be of great value not only to those living in these up-coast towns but to people everywhere throughout this dominion.
In closing I again reiterate my congratulations to the minister and to his predecessor for recognizing, at long last, this very essential link in the trans-Canada highway project, that is, from the Second Narrows bridge on Burrard inlet through to Horseshoe Bay.

speechtext:
The bill before the house is disappointing, I think, in that it is so limited in its application. We had hoped, from statements made in a similar discussion last year by the former minister of public works, that the government would have brought forth an over-all highway policy for this country.
There is no doubt that there is a need to extend the provisions of the Trans-Canada Highway Act in order to allow the provinces which have been slow in construction the opportunity to continue their construction so that we may at some time in the future have an adequate trans-Canada highway system. But this bill, being the government's major highway program for this year, apart from the roads to resources program, is a disappointment in the light of the promises made to the Canadian people that the government would not be satisfied with merely a continuation of the very narrow program which had been instigated by the previous administration. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made this very clear during the election campaign. He said, for example, in Toronto on February 4, 1957:
I am one of those who believe that a national highway policy should be launched to provide highways for peace, and defence highways should war come.
We are still looking for this highway policy for peace, these roads designed to provide Canada with adequate highway and road


facilities. It is certainly not contained in this present bill and it is not contained in any indication which the government has given to the house during the course of this session. As a matter of fact, when we asked whether the government was considering any extension of the trans-Canada highway program all we received was the nebulous answer: this is still under consideration, it is a question of government policy to be announced in due course. The government has no policy. Certainly no indication of any has been given so far. All we are being asked to pass is an amendment to the Trans-Canada Highway Act to provide for an aggregate expenditure of $400 million, an increase in the aggregate of $50 million.
I think there are good reasons why Canada should have a comprehensive highway program, and good reasons why the federal government should bear part of the cost of such a program. The bill before the house indicates that the government, like the former government, has accepted the principle that at least as far as one main highway in the country is concerned the dominion government should bear some financial responsibility and assume responsibility for leadership with regard to construction. I think it is very much in the national interest that there should be an extension of this program.
I am one who believes-as we thought the Prime Minister used to believe-that there is need for additional highways, or a second trans-Canada highway, if you will, or for further main arterial highways to be constructed running north and south, with federal assistance, in order to provide more adequate road facilities. I think more adequate highways are necessary for a great many reasons. I think they are necessary because of local needs of transportation, including the need of roads for school buses.

I am perfectly willing to endeavour to abide by the ruling as you have laid it down, Mr. Speaker. I was not in the chamber when Mr. Speaker made the statement to which you have referred. I do not know whether or not Your Honour was in the chamber or whether you have read it. I am not wishing to comment on it in any case. But I was informed that this ruling had to do with discussion of the details of the proposal for a second trans-Canada highway, something which I say is different from saying that we should have an over-all transportation policy to meet the needs of this country and that there should be an extension of the principles of this measure.
Trans-Canada Highway Act
The money that is being provided in this act will not accrue to all of the provinces in this country. Of those provinces that obtain money under this new act or the changed act some will, of course, receive money in much different proportion from that received by other provinces. This situation arises from the fact that a good deal of progress has been made in the building of the trans-Canada highway in some provinces and relatively little progress has been made in some other provinces.
I have in my hand the report of the proceedings under the Trans-Canada Highway Act for the last year available, namely the fiscal year ended March 31, 1959. It sets forth the construction accomplishments under this act up to that time. I am not going to quote all of the figures. I am merely going to point out that many provinces have a large mileage yet to be constructed. The province of Newfoundland has 502 miles still unpaved; Prince Edward Island has one mile. In other words, up to that time in Prince Edward Island the trans-Canada highway was almost completed. Nova Scotia had 90 miles to go, New Brunswick 72 miles, Ontario 349 miles, Manitoba 16 miles, Alberta 6 miles and British Columbia 209 miles; national parks 63 miles. Out of a total mileage through national parks of 143, the federal government had succeeded up to that time in paving just 80 miles. Saskatchewan was the only province up to that point that had completed its section of the trans-Canada highway.
We need a broader highway policy in order to make such highway facilities available to Canadians who wish to travel; to Canadians in their own business undertakings; to Canadians who need to obtain various services, some of them as important as emergency hospital and medical services.
I suggest to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) that an expenditure of money on an accelerated highway program at this time-that is accelerated in order to speed up the completion of the trans-Canada highway and to provide other main highway facilities in this country-is money well invested. I think the government should not look at money spent on the trans-Canada highway in the narrow sense of some other moneys that are currently spent in the budget. Rather, I think the money spent under this act should be considered a capital investment and, as far as our national government is concerned, a self-liquidating investment.
I am convinced that money spent on adequate highway facilities in this country-

Trans-Canada Highway Act completion of the trans-Canada highway, an auxiliary or secondary trans-Canada highway and other main north-south roads connecting with international highways in the United States-would return great dividends to the Canadian nation. Even from the revenue position of the federal government, considering the additional money that would come from tourist traffic and the additional money spent by Canadians, I am positive that this is an investment that would be very much a paying proposition.
At a time when our tourist trade is on the decline and when we have a larger and larger imbalance in our foreign accounts I would think that the government would be farsighted if it were embarking on a program of highway development in order to attract tourists into this country and in order to reduce the imbalance in Canada's international payments.
There are other reasons why an acceleration of this program would be very much in order at this time. The government cannot claim that we are not in a position to do the work, that we lack construction equipment, that we lack personnel for such a highway program. Contractors have been looking for work in recent years. We are told that some of the machinery has been idle because of lack of opportunities for construction, and we know that half a million Canadians are unemployed. Why should the country be allowed to stagnate? Why should the government not take a lead in providing necessary highway facilities when those are so obviously in the national interests of our country?
The government had a vision before the election, but the election is over and the vision has disappeared. Now we have just the same warmed-over program that the government inherited from the previous administration. We have statements made by the Prime Minister on television that representations about a second trans-Canada highway have been received, but he is not meeting the provinces on this question. As far as I have been able to find out he is not considering at this time an accelerated highway program, nor is the government considering an extension of the present measure.
I think the government should be doing everything to encourage those provinces that have so far lagged behind in construction of this highway. As the hon. member for Burna-by-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) pointed out, I think additional measures will have to be taken by the government to bolster the financial position of at least some of the provinces and that on the basis of an exact formula, a

fair formula, the government should consider increasing the amount of money paid under this act.
As far back as 1916 the United States inaugurated a federal system of roads, and in that nation because of federal leadership, they have built a system of interstate highways, state highways and local farm to market roads largely because the federal government has been paying money into the building of those roads. In Canada our vision has been narrow, it has been short. This government is paying into this highway and it is putting into the roads to resources program.
The people of the province of British Columbia can be very critical, I believe, of their own provincial government. I leave that to them. But they certainly have a legitimate claim that this government should embark on a secondary trans-Canada highway. The people of Alberta are in much the same position. The people of Manitoba think in exactly the same way. I think the people of Saskatchewan feel more aggrieved on this question than the people of any other province, because the province of Saskatchewan was the province which co-operated so well, so readily, so closely and so efficiently with the previous administration that it completed its section of the trans-Canada highway in
1957.	Since that time the government of Saskatchewan has been endeavouring to impress upon the federal government the need to embark on a more extensive highway program. There is a large file of correspondence that has been exchanged between the government of Saskatchewan and various federal ministers on this question but to no avail. Today the government of Saskatchewan stands ready and anxious. It demands a chance to co-operate with the federal government in an extension of this very program.

Average for all Canada, $45 per capita.
And it is suggested, Mr. Speaker, that Quebec, with expenditures of $26 per capita, has done its duty as far as roads are concerned.


I have here a statement from the highway transport association, which says:
The highway transport operators finally hope that Quebec come to some agreement with Ottawa, so that the province of Quebec might recover-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: Order.
