maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the latitude you have given me, and you probably did so because I was not out of order.
As I was attempting to show the proportion between the efforts made by the various provinces, and also to prove that Quebec had not done its full share, I had to mention that some important organizations in my province were hoping that an agreement might be reached between the present Minister of Public Works and the premier of Quebec. Consequently, I had to prove the importance of taking advantage of the minister's good will towards Quebec. And if the Liberals, the citizens of the province of Quebec, do not approve of the policy of the Conservative party or the Union Nationale, let at least the minister's good will towards the province of Quebec allow those sums of money which are being spent all over the country to benefit the province of Quebec as well.
I say that in Quebec, we do not have the highways we need. One of the reasons why we did not agree to the arrangement, according to the Union Nationale, is that we have excellent highways. Well, Mr. Speaker, if we have excellent highways almost everywhere, why does not the present minister ask Quebec authorities to mention those that are not excellent, so that we may know exactly where we are, and that we may do something about it.
Take for instance, the case of Montreal, which has a population of over a million people. The citizens of that city are up against great difficulties at this time. On the northern side, there is the Metropolitan boulevard, and the municipal authorities have prepared plans for a super-highway running east-west on the southern side. The trans-Canada

highway will necessarily have to go through there. Why could not the authorities of that city get some of the funds made available by the present government?
Have no fear, Mr. Speaker, I have no intention to suggest a second trans-Canada highway. Bad enough that, so far, we have no such highway at all in the province of Quebec.
However, with regard to those two highways, perhaps the present Minister of Public Works could ask the government to tell us to which of those two constructions it would be prepared to contribute. The province of Quebec could thus share in the advantages of the act, at least in Montreal, and at the same time we should know whether the additional amount of $50 million that we are asked to vote would be enough.
I understand that the Minister of Public Works has increased the amount by $50 million, for he knew full well-as he is prepared to say-that Quebec would still turn down the program, for if the Quebec government changed its mind and decided to join the program this year, and went ahead and built the 400 miles of highway called for under the act, it is not a mere $50 million that would be needed, but a hundred million dollars. Therefore, would the minister indicate whether the amount that would be needed, if Quebec did accept to join the program, is included in the $50 million added to the total amount to be spent.

However, I find myself in a fascinating position tonight. I have been invited by my good friend the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget)-he is a great friend of mine-to become a constitutional authority and to give a constitutional answer for the benefit of the loyal opposition and, I am sure, for the benefit of the opposition in the province of Quebec. I have also been asked a question by that Bob Hope of the House of Commons, that straight man, the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis).
Trans-Canada Highway Act I am honoured also to think that we can get his mind away from post office robberies and on to this subject. Even if it is not on the subject, at least he is addressing questions to me and I am really honoured. This is the first time in my career that I have drawn his attention and I am really greatly honoured. I hope he will continue. I have not had as much attention in a long time.
I am asked whether Quebec is going to participate and whether I think Quebec should participate. All I want to do in answering the hon. member for Levis and the hon. member for St. Denis is to say this. If the prime minister of Quebec, Mr. Barrette, is always as able, good, wise and charming as he was in his visit to Toronto last week when he captivated that city and that province, I think the premier of Quebec can manage his own affairs and he does not need any advice from the new Minister of Public Works for Canada.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES

speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES

speechtext: I did not quite catch the last part of the question.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Does the minister mean that if he is as good, charming, wise and popular, he will accept participation in this project?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
One of the fundamentals that I learned as a youngster-and I have never forgotten it in the practice of law-is that one should mind one's own business. I therefore do not pretend to interpret the mind of the premier of Quebec. All I can say at the present time is that we are dealing with nine provinces. Put on the horn, my friend, and listen in on this. At some time my hon. friend might try that solution himself. If he did so, we would of course be deprived of a great deal of humour in this House of Commons. I appreciate that fact.
May I say this. I know that Quebec can manage its own affairs and that Quebec certainly would not seek advice from a Torontonian. That really means something. I am sure the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) would not even suggest that anybody from Quebec should ask advice from Ontario.
May we tonight come back to realities just for a few minutes. We have not discussed this subject since some of the hon. members of

Trans-Canada Highway Act the government here followed the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickers-gill). This has been a heyday. It has been a picnic. We have had a lovely time on constitutional rights, the interpretation of the mind of the premier of the province of Quebec, second highways, extra highways, this, that and the other thing, plus all-round condemnation with trenchant blows from that conqueror from Assiniboia who has just returned from the hustings and who forgets always that he is in the House of Commons. May I bring him back to realities and correct him, if he will permit me to do so. He is a very good friend of mine. We are fellow sufferers. We both study French. We take French from the same professor. I admit that he is making great progress. I am a little bit jealous of him because I do not shine along that line.
But may I say to the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), so that he will not feel too hurt, that never since I became the Minister of Public Works-and that is only a period of nine months-have I ever received a request either from the Saskatchewan government or any member of the Saskatchewan cabinet for a conference. I am always open for conferences. I have sometimes five, six and up to 12 delegations a day, assisted ably by my friend, the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Tassel, who always sits in on these conferences. I cannot think of any more delightful experience than that of having a delegation from the province of Saskatchewan. I would ask my friend the hon. member for Assiniboia to extend on my behalf an invitation to the premier- the Black Douglas-or any member of the Saskatchewan government because I always like to see what makes these socialists tick.
Just to show how broadminded I am, I had a meeting with Hon. P. A. Gaglardi, minister of highways of British Columbia. He was in to see me the other day and we had a very pleasant time. I know I would do the same with Mr. Douglas. May I say this. The premier of that province did have a conference on highways with the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green). I think they discussed highways before I came in.
In connection with the province of Saskatchewan and its role, I should like to deal with that matter as I deal briefly with this bill. This is a simple bill. There is nothing to it. All we are trying to do is finish up what we started eleven years ago and is not yet finished. We are the people who are putting up a sum of money; I refer to the dominion government. Unfortunately, we have not the conduct of this highway. We check it and


when the work is done we pay our share. Whether it is finished or not, I am not going to blame anyone; but I object to hon. members of the opposition blaming the dominion government. We did not set up the manner in which this highway was to be completed. It was done by our predecessors, and I am not even blaming them for it. All I am saying is that I am attempting to complete one of the grandest enterprises entered into by Canada since Sir John A. Macdonald brought about the completion of the unification of Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific by a railway.
Let me now talk about this highway and get it cleaned up. The bill contains two simple clauses providing for $50 million more and an extension of the time. As to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, I thought I would test him out this afternoon. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) always told me that if you do not say anything he falls fairly flat; but if you interrupt him he blows up and carries on with great gusto. I therefore did not say a word to all the challenges he threw out, all the innuendoes and all the rhetoric. After about 20 minutes he just faded away. I was very happy to note that fact. As long as I am minister I shall always endeavour to use that method with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
It was a wonderful exhibition we had this afternoon of twisting and turning. The hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten), who spoke very ably today and on the resolution, spoke in the same way in 1956. He is a member from Newfoundland. I appreciate the problems of Newfoundland and I appreciated the way in which he spoke. He has been consistent throughout. But the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate for the first 20 minutes was very eloquent in support of something that he steadfastly opposed all the time he was a member of the government, namely any change in the participation on a percentage basis of the provinces and the dominion in the completion of this highway.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext: When I was attacked this afternoon by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate he could not have been serious because he argued strenuously that he did not participate in the discussions with his government but he went along with it and voted for it, and that was exactly what we are doing today. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was a member of the cabinet of that time; he was in favour of it and voted for it. We have not changed it at all.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
At that time he held a very important office in the government as parliamentary assistant to the minister of public works and this is what he had to say in reply to the request that more money should be spent by the government in this endeavour to build a trans-Canada highway to help the provincial governments. Another criticism which was made, and which is generally made under similar circumstances, was that we were not doing enough.

Trans-Canada Highway Act
Now we are doing exactly as the Liberals were doing. I continue:
Well, Mr. Chairman, we of course do appreciate the demands that are made upon provincial treasuries, but we also cannot lose sight of the fact that heavy demands are made upon the federal government for national defence and for social security measures. We frequently hear demands to increase social security measures such as family allowances, old age pensions and the pensions of superannuated civil servants.
May I interpose and say that they heard the demands but they turned a deaf ear to them. I continue with the quotation:
If we are going to meet all the requests that are made by hon. members of the opposition we certainly will have to find new sources of revenue. We will have to be practical and increase taxes. We must not lose sight of that fact.
I simply cannot understand, Mr. Chairman-
My hon. friend spoke very eloquently in English. I continue:
I simply cannot understand, Mr. Chairman, how hon. members can get up in this house and repeatedly ask for more money and in the same week accuse us of taxing the people of Canada too heavily. We will probably hear that accusation tomorrow when we resume the debate on the budget. Hon, members opposite will say that the people of Canada are too heavily taxed.
Now, the hon. member-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Are you going to cast a slur on him, too?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
You can determine yourself. These words are not a slur on him. They indicate the frame of mind of the government of the day of which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was a member. At that

time I believe the hon. member for Laurier was the chairman of the St. Lawrence seaway authority.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
What about your
own promises?

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
I am going to deal with those; I will be delighted to.
The Hon. Mr. Winters said this:
It has been suggested that federal contributions should be increased above the present level of 50 per cent. In fairness to those provinces which have made the greatest progress, any general or over-all increase beyond 50 per cent would have to be retroactive-
I hope all hon. members will follow this. I continue:
-to the dates upon which the federal-provincial agreements were signed.
I interpose this remark. That would be 1949. The quotation goes on:
Retroactive legislation of this nature gives rise to many problems and moreover I have serious doubts as to whether this approach would achieve the desired end. Further, no advantage would be gained if the federal government increased its contributions only to have the provincial governments reduce expenditures on the highway by a similar amount. maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: May I ask a question of the minister?

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Would the hon. member do so at the end of my speech? My time is limited. I should like to hear the hon. member.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: I will.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: In 1958, of course, after the Liberals had been flung from power and were getting ready for another election they switched over completely and decided that 90 per cent should be paid by the dominion and 10 per cent by the provinces. That was their convention jargon. They went to the people but the people did not take them seriously and gave them the greatest licking any political party has received since confederation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: If you carry on the way you are carrying on now you may get a licking.

maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext: You forget that there is always another election coming.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND PERIOD OF PAYMENTS AND INCREASE MAXIMUM EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
There is always another election coming and my friend will note that according to the Gallup poll we would get 180 seats if there was an election tomorrow. Could this scheme have been changed? Perhaps it could have been changed in 1956 but could it be changed now? Up to 1956 only $225 million of work had been approved for construction. I should like your attention to this matter, Mr. Speaker, because

I want to emphasize this point. In the period from 1956 to 1960, $313 million more work was approved for construction. So you can see that with that tremendous sum expended it is too late to change the percentages in 1960 when three of the provinces have practically completed the work, when others will have completed it very shortly, most of them, we hope, by the end of 1963. We agree with the minister of public works of that day- hon. members will appreciate this-that any over-all increase would have to be retroactive to 1949 to cover all the provinces, including the province of Saskatchewan from which the hon. member for Assiniboia comes. To do otherwise would be discriminatory and that is something of which the Diefenbaker government can never properly be accused.
It would involve paying all the provinces on a 90 per cent basis and would require an increase of $265 million in federal funds- think of it, $265 million-so that the Atlantic provinces could be treated on a 90 per cent basis as was suggested by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I do not think there is an hon. member in the house from any one of the 10 provinces who would suggest that an act such as the Trans-Canada Highway Act, which required each of the provinces to enter into a contract similar in every paragraph except as to the schedule of work to be done, should be changed unless all provinces were going to be treated alike. How could you change the contracts of one, two, three or four provinces without changing the contracts of all provinces? It would be an impossible situation, that $265 million more than has already been provided should be spent by the federal government so that some of the shortcomings which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate claims have been perpetrated on certain provinces can be corrected. One cannot change the percentage for one of the nine participating provinces without making the same change for the other provinces. Each one of them had an obligation to complete the share of the trans-Canada highway within their own borders and when they had completed the share within their own borders and had been paid by the dominion government they had been dealt with fairly, could require nothing more and could not claim that they had been dealt with unfairly.

It has been dealt with fairly under the terms of the Trans-Canada Highway Act.
So I say to hon. members that the object of this federal government-I do not claim that the former government had any other purpose-is to deal freely and fairly with all the provinces, but the federal government wants the trans-Canada highway completed and the sooner it is done the better.

speechtext: In the calendar year 1959 the number of miles approved amounted to 421 and the number completed was 270 miles.

maintopic: PAVING CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
This gives us a very adequate picture of the progress that has been made to date. The minister has already said that of some 4,491 miles, 2,373 miles have been paved to trans-Canada standards to date. Another 800 miles have been paved, I understand, to somewhat lower provincial standards. On the basis of the mileage of road paved to trans-Canada standards, after 11 years of operation we have just over half of the total mileage paved. If one adds in the mileage paved to the lower standards we still have some 1,300 miles or so yet to be paved. I suggest that at this rate we shall be lucky if we are half way through by way of time of construction of the trans-Canada highway across this nation by 1963, and in this I am making no reference at all to the province of Quebec. For a nation like ours to take 11 years to construct approximately 50 per cent of the mileage to standard is far too slow.
I suggest to the minister that the government should have a new look at the trans-Canada highway program, and the problem that it is endeavouring to solve. I suggest that now is the time that the government, as a government, should do some of the things necessary to speed up construction, to make more money available to the provinces so that this highway can be completed and in use before too many more years go by.
I hope I am pessimistic; I mean, I hope I am too pessimistic, I hope my pessimism is not borne out by events, but it looks to me as if we shall be back in parliament a few years from now considering a further extension of this act because with the leadership, or the lack of leadership, I should say, given to this problem by the federal government I see little hope of a completed trans-Canada highway being available to Canadians even as late as the end of 1963.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: PAVING CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for these pertinent questions. My answer is this. When the hon. member is away from the house making political speeches-and as the leader of that party I think he should do that-I shall be grateful to have his assistance in whatever province he goes in stirring them up and encouraging them to complete their particular part of the highway. After all, we can only do that. We have opened up this offer and we say, "Now here it is, boys; we will pay you when you deliver." We pay them as soon as they deliver, and all I can tell my hon. friend in reply to his inquiry as to whether or not this highway will be completed by the end of 1963 is that the plans of each of the provinces, with the exception of Newfoundland, call for the completion of its share of the highway before 1963.
Before coming to this house with this legislation we had our departmental inspectors right across the country make inquiries as to that and that is why we were able to come to the house and make the proposition that we make tonight. I must admit, however, that we are relying on the information that we have from the provinces. In view of the enthusiasm of my hon. friend and other members, I am sure they will encourage the provinces to complete their own program by the end of 1963.

As far as Premier Bennett is concerned, I do not know what he has said recently but I saw his inimitable minister of highways less than a week ago and if he had any complaints I am sure that in our hour-long interview he would have mentioned them. He did not utter a word of complaint.

speechtext: I am under strict instructions from the Chairman to keep in order and he has declared this discussion out of order. With the greatest respect, as the humble Minister of Public Works I do not think you should ask me a question like that. I am burdened with cares. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
It is very good of the hon. member to have such consideration for me and the comments I have made. I had a very pleasant interview of over an hour with the minister of highways of British Columbia. He told me in parting that he had thoroughly enjoyed himself, that I had answered some questions and that he would like to be in the same party as myself. That was an invitation for me to join the Social Credit party and he did not offer to join the Conservatives. We had a very pleasant time and the only time that I had to say no was to his suggestion that I should amend what I had said in the house with regard to a second trans-Canada highway. I had to tell him, of course, that that was a question of government policy and, like the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, we did not feel that this was the time to contemplate a second trans-Canada highway or even to consider it when we are so far from completion of the first trans-Canada highway.
He was disappointed because he said they had a program in British Columbia and would like to chisel in on the federal government for some more funds. I asked him if he got more funds would he still take credit for all the highways that were built with federal money? Signs have been put up all over indicating that highways have been built by the provincial government and Mr. Gag-lardi's name is prominently displayed at the bottom of these signs. All in all, it was a very pleasant visit, but although we have

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will try to make an honest attempt and I thank my hon. friend for making that reference. My hon. friend has drawn a long bow and is trying to make a comparison where there is none. My hon. friend, who is an astute lawyer and a much more astute politician, I think can appreciate that it would be folly for me to

attempt a positive answer to something which must be completely hypothetical because the terms of any contract which might be entered into with the province of Quebec are something which I could not even contemplate at the present time, and something which has not been given any consideration by me.
